title: The 把 construction: doing something to a known object
summary: 把 pulls a definite object in front of the verb so that the sentence can say what is done to it and where it ends up. It is the standard way to report a result, a change of place or a transformation.
pattern: Subject + 把 + Object + Verb + Complement / 了 / 在 + Place / 给 + Person

rules.rule: The core idea is **disposal**: the speaker handles a specific thing and says what happens to it. The object is named first (after 把), then the verb tells the effect. English would say "finish the homework"; Chinese says "take the homework, finish it".

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ zuòyè zuòwán le.
examples.english: I finished my homework.

examples.pinyin: Tā bǎ nà bēi chá hē le.
examples.english: He drank that cup of tea.

rules.rule: The verb can **never stand bare**. It needs something after it: a result complement, 了, a direction, a place phrase (在 / 到), a recipient (给), a short quantity (一下) or reduplication.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ mén dǎkāi.
examples.english: Please open the door.

examples.hanzi: 你把这个句子再读一遍。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ bǎ zhè ge jùzi zài dú yí biàn.
examples.english: Read this sentence once more.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xiān bǎ zhuōzi cā cā.
examples.english: First wipe the table down.

rules.rule: Movement and giving are the classic territory: **把 + object + 放在 / 带到 / 送给 + place or person**. Without 把 these verbs cannot take the destination after the object.

examples.pinyin: Tā bǎ shū fàngzài zhuōzi shang.
examples.english: He put the book on the table.

examples.hanzi: 我想把这份礼物送给你。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng bǎ zhè fèn lǐwù sònggěi nǐ.
examples.english: I would like to give you this present.

rules.rule: Change of form or identity: 把…翻译成, 把…变成, 把…当作, 把…叫做. The object is transformed into, or treated as, something else.

examples.hanzi: 请把这句话翻译成英文。
examples.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ zhè jù huà fānyì chéng yīngwén.
examples.english: Please translate this sentence into English.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yìzhí bǎ tā dàngzuò péngyǒu.
examples.english: I have always regarded him as a friend.

contrasts.text: 我做完了作业 and 我把作业做完了 mean nearly the same. 把 puts the stress on what happened to the object and is preferred whenever there is a destination or a transformation.
Both put the object before the verb. 把 keeps the doer as subject (他把杯子打破了); 被 makes the affected thing the subject (杯子被他打破了).

pitfalls: ✗ 我把作业做。 → ✓ 我把作业做完了。 The verb after 把 needs a complement or 了.
✗ 我把没做完作业。 → ✓ 我没把作业做完。 Negatives and modals go before 把, not before the verb.
✗ 他放书在桌子上。 → ✓ 他把书放在桌子上。 / 他把书放在了桌子上。 A destination needs 把 or a topic object.
✗ 我把一本书看完了。 → ✓ 我把那本书看完了。 The 把 object must be a known, specific thing.

title: Limits of 把: which sentences cannot use it
summary: 把 is not an optional style choice. The object must be definite, the verb must really affect it, and the verb must not be bare. When these fail, use ordinary Subject-Verb-Object order.
pattern: ✓ Subject + 把 + definite Object + Verb + something  ·  ✗ 把 with 有 / 是 / 喜欢 / 看见 / 知道

rules.rule: The object of 把 must be **definite**: something both speaker and listener can identify (这本书, 那个人, 我的包). Indefinite objects like "a book" are not allowed.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ nà běn shū kànwán le.
examples.english: I finished reading that book.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ kànwán le yì běn shū.
examples.english: I finished reading a book.

rules.rule: The verb must be **active and transitive**, producing a result or a movement. Verbs of existence, identity, feeling, perception or knowing (有, 是, 在, 喜欢, 爱, 怕, 知道, 觉得, 看见, 听见, 像) never take 把.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xǐhuan zhè jiàn yīfu.
examples.english: I like this piece of clothing very much.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ kànjiàn le nǐ de gēge.
examples.english: I saw your brother.

examples.pinyin: Tā zhīdào zhè jiàn shì.
examples.english: He knows about this matter.

rules.rule: Potential complements and bare verbs are excluded because 把 requires a realised outcome, not an ability. Say 我看不懂这本书, never 把…看不懂.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ kàn bu dǒng zhè běn shū.
examples.english: I cannot understand this book.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ zhè běn shū kàndǒng le.
examples.english: I have understood this book.

rules.rule: **Negation, 不能 / 应该 / 想 / 要 and time adverbs go before 把.** 把 plus its verb is a single block that cannot be broken up.

examples.pinyin: Tā méi bǎ yàoshi dàilái.
examples.english: He did not bring the keys.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ yīnggāi bǎ yào chī le.
examples.english: You should take the medicine.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng bǎ fángjiān dǎsǎo yíxià.
examples.english: I want to tidy the room a bit.

contrasts.text: Indefinite things come after the verb (我买了一本书). If you can add 这 or 那 naturally, 把 becomes possible.
English "I took the news badly" can be disposed of; Chinese 我知道这件事 can never become 我把这件事知道. The verb must change or move the object.

pitfalls: ✗ 我把他喜欢。 → ✓ 我喜欢他。 Feelings and states are never disposal.
✗ 我把一个朋友遇到了。 → ✓ 我遇到了一个朋友。 Indefinite object; use ordinary order.
✗ 他把门不关。 → ✓ 他没把门关上。 / 他不关门。 Negative before 把 or drop 把.
✗ 我把问题没有解决。 → ✓ 我没有把问题解决。 Put 没有 before 把.

title: The passive with 被, 叫, 让 and 给
titleHanzi: 被 · 叫 · 让 · 给
summary: 被 turns the affected thing into the subject: 钱包被偷了 (the wallet was stolen). 叫, 让 and 给 do the same in speech, but they require the agent to be named.
pattern: Patient + 被 (+ Agent) + Verb + Complement / 了  ·  Patient + 叫 / 让 + Agent + Verb + Complement

rules.rule: Start with the thing affected, add **被**, optionally the doer, then a verb with a result or 了. As with 把, the verb must not be bare.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le.
examples.english: My wallet was stolen.

examples.pinyin: Tā bèi lǎoshī pīpíng le.
examples.english: He was criticised by the teacher.

rules.rule: In everyday speech **叫** and **让** replace 被. They are less formal and **require** the agent to be mentioned (even if vague, like 人 "someone"). 被 may omit the agent.

examples.hanzi: 我的自行车让人骑走了。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ de zìxíngchē ràng rén qízǒu le.
examples.english: My bike was taken away by somebody.

examples.pinyin: Bēizi jiào dìdi dǎsuì le.
examples.english: The cup was broken by my little brother.

rules.rule: **给** can also mark the passive in colloquial speech, or it can be added after 被 / 让 / 叫 as an extra emphasis on the (usually unwelcome) event.

examples.hanzi: 我的手机被小偷给偷走了。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi xiǎotōu gěi tōuzǒu le.
examples.english: My phone was stolen by a thief.

examples.pinyin: Zhè bēi kāfēi gěi wǒ hē guāng le.
examples.english: I drank this whole cup of coffee.

rules.rule: **Negation, modals and adverbs** go before 被. Positive uses are common too: 被选为, 被评为, 被邀请.

examples.pinyin: Yīfu méi bèi yǔ línshī.
examples.english: The clothes did not get wet in the rain.

examples.pinyin: Tā bèi xuǎn wèi bānzhǎng.
examples.english: He was chosen as class monitor.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bù xiǎng bèi biérén kànjiàn.
examples.english: I do not want to be seen by others.

contrasts.text: 把 keeps the doer as subject (他打碎了杯子 → 他把杯子打碎了); 被 puts the receiver first (杯子被他打碎了). Choose 被 when the focus is on what happened to the receiver.
让 can mean "let / make" (妈妈让我去). It is a passive only when followed by an agent and then a complete verb: 杯子让弟弟打碎了. Look for a result complement.

pitfalls: ✗ 钱包被偷。 → ✓ 钱包被偷了。 The verb needs 了 or a complement.
✗ 我的自行车被骑走他。 → ✓ 我的自行车被他骑走了。 The agent goes between 被 and the verb.
✗ 杯子让打碎了。 → ✓ 杯子让弟弟打碎了。 让 and 叫 require an overt agent.
✗ 他被没老师批评。 → ✓ 他没被老师批评。 Negation goes before 被.
✗ 书被我看了。(for a plain neutral event) → ✓ 我看了这本书。 Use 被 for something that happens to the thing, not for every transitive verb.

title: Notional passives: passive meaning without 被
summary: Chinese often expresses the passive simply by putting a thing as the topic with a finished verb. 饭做好了 means "the meal has been cooked" with no 被, because only a person could have done it.
pattern: Topic (patient) + Verb + Complement / 了 / 着

rules.rule: When the subject is a **thing that obviously cannot act**, Chinese uses an active-looking verb with a complement; the passive reading is automatic. No 被 is needed (and it would often sound stiff).

examples.pinyin: Fàn zuòhǎo le.
examples.english: The meal is cooked.

examples.pinyin: Zuòyè yǐjīng xiěwán le.
examples.english: The homework has already been written.

rules.rule: The verb is typically followed by **了**, **着**, a result complement or a direction. These supply the completion that 被 would otherwise signal.

examples.pinyin: Mén kāizhe.
examples.english: The door is open.

examples.pinyin: Dēng guān le.
examples.english: The light has been turned off.

examples.pinyin: Xìn yǐjīng jìchūqù le.
examples.english: The letter has already been posted.

rules.rule: Notional passives report processes and states: construction, production, publication, repair. The agent is unknown, obvious or unimportant.

examples.pinyin: Xīn fángzi gàihǎo le.
examples.english: The new house has been built.

examples.pinyin: Zhè běn shū qùnián chūbǎn le.
examples.english: This book was published last year.

rules.rule: If the subject **could** also be the doer (people and animals), use 被 to avoid ambiguity. A sentence like 鸡不吃了 can mean "the chicken won't eat" or "the chicken is not eaten".

examples.pinyin: Jī bèi gǒu chī le.
examples.english: The chicken was eaten by the dog.

examples.pinyin: Dàngāo bèi háizimen chīwán le.
examples.english: The cake was eaten up by the children.

contrasts.text: 被 adds a feeling of something happening to the thing, often unwelcome, and usually points to an agent. Notional passives are neutral and descriptive.
这本书是他写的 stresses who wrote it. 这本书写好了 only reports the state of the book.

pitfalls: ✗ 饭被做好了。 → ✓ 饭做好了。 With a neutral event and an unnamed agent, the bare form is natural.
✗ 作业写。 → ✓ 作业写完了。 Even in notional passives the verb needs a complement or 了.
✗ 门被开着。 → ✓ 门开着。 着 describes a state; 被 is not used with it.

title: 受, 遭 and 挨: passives built with nouns
summary: 受, 遭 and 挨 say that the subject "receives" an experience, usually from an action noun: 受欢迎, 遭到批评, 挨骂. They differ in register and in how negative the experience is.
pattern: Subject + 受 / 受到 / 遭到 / 遭受 / 挨 + (Agent的) + action noun / verb

rules.rule: **受 / 受到** is the neutral all-rounder: the subject receives influence, education, welcome or injury. It works with good and bad things.

examples.pinyin: Zhè wèi gēshǒu hěn shòu huānyíng.
examples.english: This singer is very popular.

examples.hanzi: 这家公司受到了很大影响。
examples.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī shòudào le hěn dà yǐngxiǎng.
examples.english: This company has been greatly affected.

rules.rule: **遭 / 遭到 / 遭受** is for **bad** things and sounds formal: criticism, attack, loss, disaster, rejection. Newspapers use it constantly.

examples.hanzi: 他的建议遭到了大家的反对。
examples.pinyin: Tā de jiànyì zāodào le dàjiā de fǎnduì.
examples.english: His proposal met with everybody's opposition.

examples.hanzi: 公司遭受了巨大的损失。
examples.pinyin: Gōngsī zāoshòu le jùdà de sǔnshī.
examples.english: The company suffered enormous losses.

rules.rule: **挨** is colloquial and always unpleasant: 挨骂, 挨打, 挨批评, 挨饿. It takes a bare noun or verb and often an object like 一顿.

examples.hanzi: 他因为迟到挨了老师一顿骂。
examples.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi chídào āi le lǎoshī yí dùn mà.
examples.english: He got a scolding from the teacher for being late.

examples.pinyin: Háizi shuōhuǎng āi dǎ le.
examples.english: The child got a beating for lying.

rules.rule: Compare with 被: these verbs need an action **noun** (批评, 影响, 欢迎), not a full verb phrase, and the agent appears with 的 before the noun (受到老师的批评).

examples.pinyin: Tā shòudào le lǎoshī de pīpíng.
examples.english: He was criticised by the teacher.

examples.pinyin: Tā bèi lǎoshī pīpíng le.
examples.english: He was criticised by the teacher.

contrasts.text: 被 requires a verb (被批评); 受到 / 遭到 take the noun (受到批评). The meaning is the same, but 受到 sounds more written and 遭到 more negative.
These cover positive receiving (得到帮助, 获得好评). 受 is neutral, 遭 and 挨 are negative; choosing the right one tells the reader how the writer feels.

pitfalls: ✗ 他受到老师。 → ✓ 他受到老师的批评。 A bare person cannot be the thing received.
✗ 他挨了很多快乐。 → ✓ 他得到了很多快乐。 挨 is only for unpleasant things.
✗ 他被受到批评了。 → ✓ 他受到了批评。 / 他被批评了。 Do not stack 被 and 受到.
✗ 公司遭到了成功。 → ✓ 公司取得了成功。 遭 is never for good outcomes.
